seo.title: Beam Deflection Calculator - Free Online Structural Tool
seo.description: Calculate beam deflection under load — Simply supported & cantilever beams using standard formulas

formula.explanation: Maximum deflection delta = P * L^3 / (k * E * I), where k = 48 for a simply supported beam with a central point load and k = 3 for a cantilever with an end point load. The engine converts length to meters (m) and modulus to pascals (Pa); moment of inertia is entered in mm^4 and converted to m^4 (1 mm^4 = 1e-12 m^4). The result is multiplied by 1000 to express deflection in millimeters.

content.introduction: Calculate the maximum deflection of a beam under a point load for two common support conditions: a simply supported beam with the load at midspan, and a cantilever beam with the load at the free end. The calculator uses the classic elastic flexure formula delta = P*L^3 / (k*E*I), where P = point load (N), L = span (m), E = modulus of elasticity (Pa), I = second moment of area (m4), and k is a support-condition constant (48 for simply supported center load, 3 for cantilever end load). Results are in millimeters and assume linear-elastic, small-deflection behavior with a prismatic beam. This Tool + Formula + Example + Guide page supports beam sizing checks, serviceability verification, and structural education.

example.description: A 3 m simply supported steel beam (E=200,000 MPa, I=1e6 mm^4) under a 10 kN center load deflects 28.125 mm at midspan.

faq.q: What is the modulus of elasticity of steel?
faq.a: Carbon structural steel has a modulus of elasticity of approximately 200,000 MPa (200 GPa). Stainless steel is similar, around 193,000 MPa.

faq.q: How do I find the moment of inertia I?
faq.a: The second moment of area depends on the cross-section shape. For a rectangular section b wide and h deep, I = b*h^3/12. For standard steel sections, use published section properties (e.g. I-beam, W-shape tables).

faq.q: What are the limits of this calculator?
faq.a: It assumes linear-elastic material behavior, small deflections, a prismatic beam, and a single point load. It does not account for self-weight, shear deformation, or partial fixity; for complex loading use a full frame or FEA analysis.

faq.q: What deflection limit should I check against?
faq.a: Common serviceability limits are span/360 for total load or span/240 for live load, but always verify against the governing code (e.g. AISC, ACI, Eurocode) and project specification.

faq.q: How do I convert beam deflection from mm to inches?
faq.a: Multiply the deflection in mm by 0.03937. For example, 28.125 mm = 1.107 inches. Conversely multiply inches by 25.4 to get mm.

faq.q: What is a typical deflection limit for steel beams?
faq.a: A common rule is span/360 for total load and span/240 to span/360 for live load only. For a 6 m span that means roughly 16.7 mm maximum. Crane girders and sensitive flooring are stricter (L/600 or tighter). Always check AISC, ACI, or Eurocode for the applicable limit.

faq.q: Can this calculator handle uniformly distributed loads?
faq.a: The interactive tool models a single point load (centre load for simply supported, end load for cantilever). For distributed load w (N/m), use delta = 5wL^4/(384EI) for a simply supported beam, or wL^4/(8EI) for a cantilever, with consistent SI units.

sections.heading: Load Cases & Deflection Formulas
sections.body:
Simply supported beam, point load at midspan: delta = P x L^3 / (48 x E x I).
Cantilever beam, point load at free end: delta = P x L^3 / (3 x E x I).
Simply supported beam, uniformly distributed load w (N/m): delta = 5 x w x L^4 / (384 x E x I). Use this approximation when the dominant load is distributed (floors, platforms) rather than a single point load.
Cantilever, uniformly distributed load: delta = w x L^4 / (8 x E x I).
All formulas assume elastic material behaviour, small deflections, and constant cross-section (prismatic beam).

sections.heading: Worked Design Example: Steel Floor Beam
sections.body:
Check a 6 m simply supported steel beam (UB 305 x 165 x 40, I = 87,300,000 mm4) under a 12 kN centre load. E = 200,000 MPa.
delta = 12,000 x 6.0^3 / (48 x 200,000 x 87.3 x 10^-6) = 2,592,000 / 838,080,000 = 0.00309 m = 3.1 mm.
Allowable deflection L/360 = 6,000 / 360 = 16.7 mm. Actual 3.1 mm < 16.7 mm, so the beam satisfies the serviceability limit with large margin.

sections.heading: Deflection Limits for Structural Design
sections.body:
Typical serviceability limits (verify against governing code and project spec):
Floor beams, total load: L/240 to L/360. Floor beams, live load only: L/360 to L/480.
Roof purlins and girts: L/180 to L/240. Crane runway girders: L/600 to L/1000 (often governed by crane manufacturer).
Industrial platforms and mezzanines: L/360 total load is common. Precast or brittle cladding systems require tighter limits to avoid cracking.
In US practice AISC recommends L/360 for floors; Eurocode EN 1993-1-1 suggests L/300 to L/360 for floors depending on occupancy.

sections.heading: Unit Conversion Guide
sections.body:
Force: 1 N = 0.2248 lbf; 1 kN = 224.8 lbf; 10 kN ≈ 2,248 lbf.
Length: 1 mm = 0.03937 in; 1 m = 3.281 ft.
Modulus: 1 MPa = 0.145 ksi; steel E = 200 GPa ≈ 29,000 ksi; aluminum E = 69 GPa ≈ 10,000 ksi.
Moment of inertia: 1 mm4 = 2.402 x 10^-6 in4.
To use US inputs with this SI engine, convert lbf to N (x 4.4482), inches to mm (x 25.4), ksi to MPa (x 6.8948).
